## Small arithmetic


### `dbGain`

```
dbGain : Float -> Float
```

`clamp lo hi x` — hold a value between a low and a high bound.

An amount in decibels as a multiplier.  `dbGain 0.0` is 1.0.


### `keyHz`

```
keyHz : Int -> Float
```

MIDI key number to hertz.  Key 69 is 440 Hz, and each semitone is the
twelfth root of two.


### `centsHz`

```
centsHz : Float -> Float -> Float
```

Detune in cents.  A hundred cents is a semitone.


### `secondsSince`

```
secondsSince : Int -> Int -> Float
```

`secondsSince n from` — how long, in seconds, instant `n` is after the
1-based instant `from`.  `audio.ges`'s `seconds` is the other direction — a duration into a count
of samples — and between them they are the whole conversion between the
two clocks a program thinks in.


### `nyquist`

```
nyquist : Float
```

The highest frequency this sample rate can carry, less a margin.

One place for the Nyquist limit, because every filter here has to clamp
its cutoff to it: `tan` blows up at half the sample rate, and a cutoff
that arrives from a knob has nothing else stopping it.


## Oscillators


### `phase`

```
phase : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

The turn number, 0..1, running at a frequency.  For a shape this file
does not already wrap — otherwise reach for `sine` and the rest.


### `sine`

```
sine : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A sine.  The shortest thing this file can say.


### `saw`

```
saw : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```


### `square`

```
square : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```


### `triangle`

```
triangle : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```


### `pulse`

```
pulse : Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A pulse of the given width — `pulse 0.5` is `square`.  Narrower widths
thin it towards a spike, and the harmonic content moves with the width,
which is what makes it worth having separately.


### `pulseOf`

```
pulseOf : Float -> Float -> Float
```

A pulse as a *shape* — the one `audio.ges` does not have.


### `unipolar`

```
unipolar : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

−1..1 to 0..1.  A modulation depth usually wants this — `mix lo hi
(unipolar (sine 5.0))` reads as the range it sweeps — and it replaces
the old `lfoAt`, which was named for its frequency when what differed
was its polarity, and worked on one shape when this works on any.


### `bipolar`

```
bipolar : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

0..1 back to −1..1 — `unipolar`'s inverse.


## Noise


### `Seed`  <sub>type alias</sub>

```
type Seed = Int
```

**Which stream of randomness.**  Any integer will do and no two are
alike; what matters is that the same one gives the same sound twice,
which is what makes a render reproducible and an oracle possible.

An alias rather than a type of its own: it is an `Int` and arithmetic on
it is meaningful (`seed + 1` is a perfectly good second stream).  What
the name buys is a signature that says *which* integer is wanted —
`dust : Seed -> Sig Float -> Sig Float` reads, and
`dust : Int -> Sig Float -> Sig Float` does not.


### `white`

```
white : Seed -> Sig Float
```

**White noise** — flat, and the source the four colours below filter.

Give two of them different seeds and they are uncorrelated, which is
what a stereo noise bed needs.  Named for its colour rather than for
being noise, now that there are five of those: `white 1` beside
`pink (white 1)` reads as one family.


### `dust`

```
dust : Seed -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**Random impulses at an average rate** — SuperCollider's `Dust`.

`dust 20.0` fires about twenty times a second, at unpredictable
instants, each impulse a value in 0.0 .. 1.0 and every other sample
zero.  It is the sparse counterpart of `white`: where white noise is a
texture, this is *events*, and what it is for is triggering things —
multiply it into a percussive envelope, or feed it to a resonant filter
and the filter rings once per impulse.

**The density is a signal**, so it can move: `dust (5.0 + 40.0 *
unipolar (sine 0.2))` thickens and thins over five seconds, which is a
shape you would otherwise have to write a sequencer for.  A literal is
already a constant signal, so `dust 20.0` costs nothing extra.

One draw of the generator decides both whether an impulse happens and
how large it is, which is what `Dust` does and is why the impulses are
uniform rather than all the same height.

The seed comes first, as `white`'s does: two `dust` at one density are
the *same* impulses unless they are seeded apart, and a drum kit whose
four voices fire together is not a kit.


## Colouring noise


### `pink`

```
pink : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

−3 dB/octave.  **The one that sounds even** — equal energy per octave
rather than per hertz, which is how hearing is spaced, so pink noise is
the noise that does not seem to lean towards the top.

Three one-pole filters summed, which is Paul Kellet's approximation:
within about a tenth of a decibel across the audible range, and three
multiply-adds rather than the octave-band bank the exact answer needs.


### `brown`

```
brown : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

−6 dB/octave.  White noise integrated — the slope of a river, distant
thunder, wind.

`lowpassOnePole` at 20 Hz *is* the leaky integrator this wants, and
writing it that way is what makes the colour right at every sample rate
rather than at the one the coefficient was picked for.  The gain goes
as √rate because an integrator's output does, which is the one place a
filter here has to know what rate it is running at.


### `violet`

```
violet : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

+6 dB/octave.  The first difference — white noise differentiated, which
is all treble and the harshest of the four.


### `blue`

```
blue : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

+3 dB/octave.  `violet (pink s)`, and that is not a trick: differentiating
adds six decibels an octave to pink's minus three.


## Envelopes


### `Adsr`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Adsr := Adsr Float Float Float Float
```

Attack, decay, sustain, release.  The three times are in seconds; the
sustain is a level in 0.0 .. 1.0.

`adsr` is what turns one of these into a signal.


### `adsrOf`

```
adsrOf : Adsr -> Int -> Int -> Int -> Float
```

`adsrOf env n on off` — the envelope's level at instant `n`, for a note
that began at `on` and was released at `off`.

**The whole envelope, as arithmetic.**  `adsr` is this with the
instants read off a `Sig Gate`, and is what a `voices` bank wants; this
is the one to reach for when you already know when the note is —
`sine.ges` holds one note between two constants and needs no `scan` of
its own because of it.


### `percOf`

```
percOf : Float -> Int -> Int -> Float
```

A one-shot exponential decay — the envelope a plucked or struck sound
wants, which does not sustain and does not care when the key came up.
The rate is how many e-foldings a second.  `perc` is its signal form.


### `adsr`

```
adsr : Adsr -> Sig Gate -> Sig Float
```

The note's envelope, from its own timing.  **The one that removes the
bookkeeping**: `on`, `off` and the instant were what a voice carried a
counter for, and all three are here.


### `perc`

```
perc : Float -> Sig Gate -> Sig Float
```

The one-shot decay, the same way — for a struck or plucked voice, which
does not sustain and does not care when the key came up.


### `onset`

```
onset : Sig Gate -> Sig Int
```

When the note began, as a signal — for a voice whose own state is a fold
over the instant rather than a function of it.


### `slew`

```
slew : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

`slew rate target` — move toward the target at that rate.  **Both are
signals**, so both may evolve.

`adsr` is a pure function of three integers: it recomputes the whole
curve every sample, which is what makes it cheap and exact.  What that
costs is that its shape cannot *change* while a note sounds — give it a
new decay halfway through and the level jumps to wherever the new curve
says it should be, which is a click.

This is the other kind of envelope, and the one a knob can turn.  It
has state, so it moves *toward* what you ask rather than *to* it, and
its output changes by at most `rate` per sample — so nothing you ask of it
can make it jump.  It is the same one-pole `audio.ges`'s `lowpass` is,
with the coefficient let out.

A portamento is `slew rate (!hzOf s)`, a smoothed knob is
`slew 0.001 level`, and an ADSR whose segments move is a target of 1,
the sustain, or 0 by stage, at that stage's rate.


## Filters


### `lowpassOnePole`

```
lowpassOnePole : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A gentle 6 dB/octave lowpass, by frequency rather than by coefficient.

Named for its circuit like the others: `audio.ges`'s `lowpass` is the
same filter taking a raw *coefficient*, which is an implementation
detail rather than a thing a musician asks for, and it keeps the plain
name because twenty-one files already spell it that way.


### `highpassOnePole`

```
highpassOnePole : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Its complement: what the lowpass took away.


### `dcBlock`

```
dcBlock : Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Remove the constant offset a rectified or asymmetric waveshaper leaves.
Not decoration — a DC offset costs headroom and does not make a sound,
so it is loudness thrown away.


### `lowpassSvf`

```
lowpassSvf : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A resonant lowpass.  The ordinary way to use the SVF.

**The cutoff is a signal, and a number is one.**  `lowpassSvf 800.0 0.4
voice` is a fixed filter and `lowpassSvf (220.0 + 2600.0 * adsr
filtEnv g) 0.4 voice` is a sweep — the same function, because a literal
is a constant signal (`Floating (Sig Float)`) and
`audioextract._fold_constants` folds it back into the step, so the fixed
form costs what a fixed form should.  There used to be a separate
`sweepSvf` for the second, and it was this written twice.

The resonance stays a `Float`: one that moves is rare, and it reaches
the step as a folded constant either way.


### `bandpassSvf`

```
bandpassSvf : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Only the band around the cutoff — the resonant peak on its own.


### `highpassSvf`

```
highpassSvf : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Everything above the cutoff.


### `notchSvf`

```
notchSvf : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

Everything *except* the band around the cutoff — the fourth response the
one state already computes, and the one a phaser is built from.


### `lowpassLadder`

```
lowpassLadder : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A four-pole lowpass — steeper than the SVF, and its resonance thins the
bass as it climbs, which is the character rather than a defect.

The cutoff is a signal here for the reason it is on `lowpassSvf`, and
`sweepLadder` is gone for the same one.


### `resonate`

```
resonate : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A struck resonance** — a frequency, how long it takes to die away, and
whatever is exciting it.

    resonate 440.0 3.0 strike

The decay is in **seconds to −60 dB**, which is how a physical object's
ring is measured and quoted.  A bell is 3 to 10, a marimba bar about
0.5, a drum head about 0.2, a woodblock 0.05.

This is what modal synthesis is made of: an object that has been struck
is a sum of these, one per mode, each at its own frequency and its own
decay.  `examples/audio/bell.ges`, `bar.ges` and `membrane.ges` are the
same four lines with different numbers in them, and the numbers are the
instrument.

Two poles and no zeros, normalised so the peak of the impulse response
is about 1 — measured 0.87 at a 0.05 s decay rising to 0.998 at 3 s, and
0.97 to 0.99 across the range from 110 Hz to 1760 Hz.  So a mode's level
is the number you multiply it by rather than a number you discover.  Unlike `bandpassSvf` it **will** ring for
minutes if asked, which also means a decay long enough and an excitation
loud enough will pile up; `limit` after a bank of them is not optional.


## Saturation and shaping


### `softClip`

```
softClip : Float -> Float
```

A soft limiter: linear near zero, curving into ±1 rather than folding.

`x - x³/3` is the cubic every analogue emulation starts from — it adds
only odd harmonics, so it thickens without sounding rectified — held
flat beyond the point where the cubic would turn back down.


### `driveOf`

```
driveOf : Float -> Float -> Float
```

Drive into the soft clipper and back out at a matched level, so turning
the amount up changes the *tone* rather than only the volume.


### `drive`

```
drive : Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

The same, as a signal transformation.


### `wrapFold`

```
wrapFold : Float -> Float
```

Fold the signal back on itself instead of limiting it — harsh, metallic,
and completely unlike `softClip` at the same input level.


## Dynamics


### `follow`

```
follow : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A peak envelope follower** — how loud the signal has been, lately.

`follow 0.005 0.2 s` rises to a new peak in about 5 ms and falls away
over about 200 ms, which is roughly how a VU meter behaves and exactly
what a compressor's detector is.  Useful on its own: a side-chain, a
level meter, an auto-wah (`lowpassSvf (200.0 + 4000.0 * follow …)`).

Times are in **seconds**, and asymmetric on purpose: a detector that
rose and fell at the same rate would either miss transients or chatter.


### `Comp`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Comp := Comp Float Float Float Float
```

A compressor's settings, as one value — the shape `Adsr` and `Patch`
already use for the same reason.

`Comp threshold ratio attack release`, with the threshold **linear**
rather than in decibels (0.5 is −6 dB; `dbGain (0.0 - 6.0)` writes it
that way if you prefer) and the ratio the usual n:1 — 4.0 is gentle,
20.0 is a limiter.


### `compress`

```
compress : Comp -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**Turn down what is loud**, by the ratio, above the threshold.

    compress (Comp 0.3 4.0 0.005 0.15) mix

Hard knee, feed-forward, peak-detecting: the plainest compressor there
is, and the one whose behaviour you can predict from its numbers.  It
applies **no makeup gain** — the output is quieter than the input by
construction, and multiplying by a number afterwards is a thing you can
see rather than a thing this does behind your back.


### `limit`

```
limit : Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

A limiter: the same compressor with the ratio turned up and the attack
turned down, because "stop it going over 0.5" is what a master bus
wants and spelling the numbers out every time invites a wrong one.

**It approaches the ceiling; it does not guarantee it.**  Measured
against a 220 Hz sine and a ceiling of 0.5: four times over comes out
at 0.541 and ten times over at 0.571, so the overshoot grows slowly and
does not run away.
Two reasons, and both are the topology rather than the numbers: a
finite ratio always lets a little through, and a peak detector's
envelope sags between the peaks of a low note, so the gain is loosest
exactly where the waveform is climbing again.  Faster ballistics do not
fix the second — measured across three settings, the overshoot did not
move.

A brick wall needs **lookahead**, and `brickwall` below is it.  This one
is kept because a limiter that does not delay the signal is the one a
live path wants: `brickwall` costs 2 ms of latency, and there are places
that is worse than an overshoot.  `clip` after this is still a hard
bound if you want one without the delay.


### `brickwall`

```
brickwall : Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A brick-wall limiter** — `limit` that sees the peak coming.

    brickwall ceiling s

The gain is computed from the signal and applied to a copy delayed by
2 ms, so it is already down by the time the peak arrives instead of
chasing it.  That is the one thing `limit` cannot do and the reason it
overshoots.

**The bound is guaranteed by the `clip` at the end, not by the
limiter**, and that is worth being blunt about because the first version
of this had no clip and did not hold: a 220 Hz sine came out at the
ceiling, and the first piece of real music put through it — drums, so
transients of well under a millisecond — went **2.71 in, 1.93 out**.
Two reasons, both structural.  A peak follower with an attack time
constant reaches 63% of a step in one of them, so an attack as long as
the lookahead has not arrived when the delayed peak does; the attack
here is 0.2 ms against 2 ms of lookahead, ten time constants, which is
caught up.  And a *finite* ratio lets the excess through divided rather
than removed — at ratio 100 a signal three times the ceiling still aims
2% above it.  The limiter's job is to make the clip rare; the clip's job
is to make the ceiling true.

**It costs 2 ms of latency**, which is not free and is why `limit` is
still there.  On a master bus it does not matter; between a key and a
sound it is the difference you can feel.


### `brickRaw`

```
brickRaw : Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

The limiter proper, before the ceiling is made true.


## Delay


### `echo`

```
echo : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**An echo.**  `echo 0.25 0.5 s` repeats `s` a quarter of a second later
at half the level, and again, and again — each repeat quieter by the
same factor.

The time is in **seconds** and folds to a sample count before the
program runs; `feedback` is what refuses one that cannot.  Feedback at
or above 1.0 never dies away and will grow without bound, so it is
clamped just below.


### `comb`

```
comb : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A comb filter** — the same line with the repeats fast enough to be
heard as a *pitch* rather than as echoes.

A delay of `1/hz` seconds fed back on itself resonates at `hz` and at
every multiple of it, which is the comb its response is named for.  At
100 Hz and above it is a tone; below about 20 it is an echo, and the
only difference is the number.

This is the resonator a plucked string is made of, and what it is
missing is a *filter* in the loop to make the high partials die first.
Without one it rings all its harmonics equally, which is a comb and not
yet a string — `string` below is that comb with the filter in it.


### `string`

```
string : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A plucked string** — Karplus-Strong, which is `comb` with an averaging
filter in the loop, and the smallest physical model there is.

    string hz decay s

`hz` is the pitch, `decay` is how many seconds it takes to fall 60 dB —
`resonate`'s parameter and the same meaning — and `s` excites it.

The pitch *is* the line's length:
a round trip of `sampleRate / hz` samples is a wave of that frequency,
so the number is fixed before the program runs, as every delay length
here is — a bent note is a `tap` with a moving position, not this.

**The length is a whole number of samples, so the pitch is quantised.**
At 44100 Hz an A at 220 asks for 200.45 samples, gets 200, and plays
220.5 — about four cents sharp, which is small.  At 8000 it asks for
36.4, gets 36, and plays 222.2, which is not.  The error grows with the
pitch and shrinks with the sample rate, and the cure is a fractional
delay: `loop` reads whole slots, `tap` interpolates.

The string keeps whatever it is handed and filters it down, so what you
excite it with is what it sounds like.  A few milliseconds of `white` is
the classic pluck; a single impulse is a much thinner tap on a wire; and
`dust` gives a string being scratched.

    stringVoice g s = string (hzOfKey s) 2.5 (white 1 * perc 400.0 g)

Averaging two neighbouring samples is a gentle lowpass, so every round
trip loses the highest partial first and the sound dies from the top
down, which is what a real string does — and it is the whole difference
between this and the `comb` underneath it.

**The `decay` is not decoration, and textbook Karplus-Strong is wrong
without it.**  The averaging filter has gain 1 at zero frequency, so
whatever DC the excitation carried circulates undamped: measured, a
noise burst at 880 Hz left the audible part gone within a third of a
second and a **−0.137 offset sitting there for good**.  That is
inaudible alone, stacks across voices, and eats headroom until it clips.
A loop gain below 1 damps it with everything else.

The gain is applied once per *round trip*, and there are `hz` of those a
second — so it is raised to the pitch before it reaches the ear.  The
exponent divides by the length again to undo that, which is what makes
`decay` mean the same **seconds** at every pitch, as `resonate`'s does.
Measured across two octaves at `decay` 2.0, the tail at 0.85 s is within
a factor of three at every pitch, where the raw filter alone left 110 Hz
ringing after 880 Hz had gone silent.

**Excite it with about one line's worth of sound.**  The string sums
whatever arrives during a round trip, so a burst longer than the line
stacks: 60 samples of noise at 0.7 into an 880 Hz string — a 9-sample
line at 8 kHz — measured a peak of **1.35**.  A short note wants a short
burst, and `clip` is there for when it does not.

Put a different filter in `loop`'s step to damp it differently — that is
what a waveguide is, and this is the shortest one.


### `allpass`

```
allpass : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A Schroeder allpass** — a delay that passes every frequency at full
strength and only rearranges *when* each arrives.

    allpass time g s

`time` is the delay in seconds and `g` how much is fed back, below 1.
Its magnitude response is flat — measured, four octaves within a few
percent of each other — so it colours nothing and smears everything,
which is exactly what a reverb needs between its combs: a comb alone
repeats at an audible rate and sounds like a corridor, and a chain of
these turns the repeats into a wash.

Alone it is nearly inaudible on a steady sound and obvious on a
transient, which is the usual way to hear phase.

The state carries two numbers because the output needs both ends of the
line at once — `v[t] = x + g * v[t-n]` and `y = v[t-n] - g * v[t]` — and
a `feedback` step only ever sees one of them.


### `damped`

```
damped : Float -> Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A comb with a lowpass in the loop** — `echo` that gets duller each
time round instead of repeating unchanged.

    damped time feedbackAmount damp s

`damp` from 0 to 1 is how much of each repeat's top end is lost on the
way round.  At 0 this is `echo`; at 0.5 a bright sound turns to a dull
one over a few repeats, which is what air and soft walls do to a room
and what makes a reverb built on it sound like a place rather than a
bucket.

**This is the case `loop` exists for.**  The filter's state has to
advance every sample while the line reaches back `n` of them, so the
step needs the state from an instant ago *and* the state from a round
trip ago — the two arms, and neither is reachable from `feedback`.


### `reverb`

```
reverb : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A room** — Schroeder's reverb, which is four damped combs in parallel
into two allpasses in series.

    reverb decay damp s

`decay` is roughly how many seconds the tail takes to fall 60 dB and
`damp` how fast the top end goes with it.  `0.25 * reverb 2.0 0.4 s`
added to `s` is a hall; the reverb alone is the wet signal and mixing it
is the caller's, because how wet a sound wants to be is a mix decision
and not a property of the room.

The four comb lengths are close together but share no common divisor —
29.7, 37.1, 41.1 and 43.7 ms — so their repeats interleave instead of
landing on top of each other.  Delays that divide evenly would ring on
one pitch, which is the difference between a room and a comb filter.

**It is not free.** Four lines of ~40 ms plus two allpasses is about
7000 samples of state at 44100 Hz, and the state is allocated whether or
not anything is sounding.


### `flanger`

```
flanger : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A flanger** — a very short delay whose length is swept by an LFO,
added back to the dry signal.

    flanger rate depth s

`rate` is the sweep in hertz — a fraction of one is the usual — and
`depth` from 0 to 1 how far it swings.  The sum of a signal and a
delayed copy of itself cancels at every frequency whose half-period the
delay matches, so a delay of a few milliseconds puts a comb across the
audible range, and moving it drags the notches through the sound.

A *fixed* position is a feedforward comb and is one line of `tap`; what
makes a flanger is that the position moves.  `chorus` is the same thing
with a longer delay, and the length is the whole difference between
them — short enough to hear as notches, or long enough to hear as a
second voice slightly out of tune.


### `chorus`

```
chorus : Float -> Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**A chorus** — `flanger` with the delay long enough to be heard as a
second player rather than as a filter.

    chorus rate depth s

25 ms rather than 5.  At that length the sweep is heard as *pitch*
rather than as notches, because a delay that is changing length is a
doppler shift — which is what two instruments not quite in tune sound
like, and why this thickens a single voice.

### `Stereo`  <sub>data</sub>

### `Num Stereo`  <sub>instance</sub>

```

```

**Two channels are a number, so they do arithmetic.**  `padMix +
bassMix` is a mix and `0.85 * mix` is a fader, which is what those two
things are — and the alternative was `mixStereo` and `gainStereo`, four
names for `+` and `*` at two types.  `audio.ges` makes the same argument
for `Sig Float`, and `spec/frp_lesson.md` is the argument itself.

`*` is componentwise, which is what a gain wants and is *not* a
meaningful "multiply two stereo signals" — there is no such operation in
audio and nothing here pretends otherwise.

What `0.85 * mix` means: the same number in both channels.

## FM


### `pm`

```
pm : Sig Float -> Sig Float -> Sig Float
```

**Phase modulation** — a carrier at `hz`, its phase shifted by `mod`.

The depth is in **turns**, like every phase in this file: `pm hz (d *
sine m)` shifts the carrier by `d` whole cycles at full modulator
swing.  Every FM tutorial you will read quotes the *index* instead,
which is radians — so an index of 2π ≈ 6.3 is a depth of 1.0, and the
useful indices of 1 to 8 are depths of about **0.15 to 1.3**.

One `map` and one addition.  It is here for the name rather than for the
work: `map sineOf (phase hz + mod)` was always legal and nothing said so.


### `pmSelf`

```
pmSelf : Sig Float -> Float -> Sig Float
```

**An operator modulating itself** — the diagonal, as one oscillator.

Feedback on a single sine sweeps it towards a sawtooth as the amount
rises, and it is the cheapest bright waveform there is.  Measured
against a plain sine at 250 Hz: an amount of 0.0 is bit-identical to
`sine`, and 0.5 is five times as bright.

A *cycle*, which `pm` cannot express — the carrier reads its own output
— so this is `feedback 1`, the one-sample delay line, with the sine
inside the loop.  Useful amounts are under about 1.0; past that it
turns to noise, which is occasionally what you want.


## The operator bank


### `Quad`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Quad := Quad Float Float Float Float
```

**A number per operator**, for operators 1, 2, 3 and 4 in that order —
the same order `Matrix`'s rows and `Patch`'s fields use.

One type used four ways on purpose, and what a number *means* depends on
which way:

| as | each number is | usual range |
|---|---|---|
| **ratios** | a multiple of the note's frequency | 0.5 to 20; whole numbers are harmonic, others are not |
| **a `Matrix` row** | how much that operator shifts this one's phase, in **turns** | 0 to 2; an index of 2π ≈ 6.3 is 1.0 |
| **levels** (what `fm` takes) | that operator's output amplitude | 0 to 1 — this is where an envelope goes |
| **amps** | how much of that operator reaches the output | 0 to 1; non-zero makes it a carrier |

**A level does two jobs, and that is the whole of why FM sounds alive.**
It multiplies an operator's sine *before* anything reads it, and both
the wiring and the output mix read the result — so on a modulator the
level is modulation depth and turning its envelope down makes the sound
**duller**, while on a carrier the same number is loudness.  An operator
that is both does both at once.  Four envelopes on four operators is
therefore a timbre that changes as the note decays, which a single
envelope over the whole bank cannot do.

Giving all four uses one name is what lets `quadDot` serve them; the
cost is that the type cannot tell you which you are holding, and
swapping ratios for amps typechecks.  It is audible immediately, which
is why it has been left that way.


### `Matrix`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Matrix := Matrix Quad Quad Quad Quad
```

One row per *target*: `Matrix r1 r2 r3 r4` and `r2`'s third component is
how much operator 3 modulates operator 2.


### `Patch`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Patch := Patch Quad Matrix Quad
```

The instrument: frequency ratios, the wiring, and how much of each
operator reaches the output.

A carrier is simply an operator with a non-zero amount here.  Nothing
marks an operator as a carrier or a modulator, because nothing needs to
— an operator can be both, and on the interesting patches it is.


### `fm`

```
fm : Patch -> Sig Float -> Sig Quad -> Sig Float
```

**The bank, as a signal transformation** — a patch, a pitch, four
levels, a sound.

    leadVoice g s = fm bellPatch (!hzOf s) (leadLevels g) * !velOf s

The second signal is the **four operator levels**, 1 to 4 in order, each
normally 0 to 1 — and that is where the envelopes go.  `Quad` says what
a level does; briefly, it scales an operator's output *before* both the
wiring and the mix read it, so on a modulator it is brightness and on a
carrier it is loudness.

Four envelopes on four operators is what makes this sound like an
instrument rather than a chord of sine waves — the timbre changes as
the note decays.  `fmpoly.ges` is four `adsrOf` calls doing exactly
that, with the modulators shorter than the carriers.

The last component of `synth.ges` to get a face, and every program that
used FM before it wrote the same eight lines: a named step because the
fragment wants one at a `scan`, a `scan` over `fmZero`, and a `map` of
`fmOut` back out.  That is the machinery, it is below `internal` now,
and this is what it was for.

**One patch, not two.**  The old shape passed it to the step *and* to
the output mix, so using two different patches in the two places
typechecked and made a sound belonging to neither.

**Two signals, not a `Drive`.**  This used to take a `Sig Drive`, which
nothing in the library produced — both examples that used FM built one
by hand, with the same `zip`, because a `scan` takes a single signal.
That is exactly what `SvfIn` is for a filter, and `SvfIn` is internal;
`lowpassSvf hz res s` takes its arguments apart and pairs them itself.
This does now too, and `Drive` has gone where the other step records
are.


### `noWiring`

```
noWiring : Matrix
```

No wiring at all — four independent sines.  Where a patch starts.


### `modulates`

```
modulates : Int -> Int -> Float -> Matrix -> Matrix
```

`modulates src dst amount` — operator `src` moves operator `dst`'s
phase by `amount` turns.  Operators are numbered 1..4.

`modulates 2 2 0.18` is **feedback**, and needs no other mechanism: the
diagonal is an operator modulating itself, which works because every
operator reads the previous sample's outputs.

A whole turn is a very large index; useful amounts are mostly under 2.


### `fmStack`

```
fmStack : Patch
```

4 → 3 → 2 → 1, and only operator 1 is heard.  The deepest algorithm a
four-operator bank has, and the one that gets metallic fastest.


### `fmBell`

```
fmBell : Patch
```

Two independent pairs, 2 → 1 and 4 → 3, both heard.  Operator 4 runs at
3.5× — a ratio that is not a whole number, which is what makes the
second pair inharmonic and the whole thing sound like a bell.


### `fmFeedback`

```
fmFeedback : Patch
```

Operator 1 modulates itself, which is the diagonal and nothing else.
Feedback on a single operator sweeps a sine towards a sawtooth as the
amount rises, and is the cheapest bright sound this bank can make.

## Internals

**Not callable from another file.**  Listed so that a name you meet in a stack trace or a definition can be looked up.


### Noise


#### `Rng`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Rng := Rng Int
```

The generator's state — one seed.


#### `rngNext`

```
rngNext : Rng -> Int -> Rng
```

`drums.ges`'s constants: a 63-bit LCG whose reach was measured rather
than assumed, because `Int` narrows to `i64` in the engine.


#### `rngOf`

```
rngOf : Rng -> Float
```

The seed as a sample in -1.0 .. 1.0.


#### `rngUnit`

```
rngUnit : Rng -> Float
```

The seed as a sample in 0.0 .. 1.0 — the same draw `rngOf` reads
bipolar, which is what lets one draw decide `dust`'s two questions.

**The high bits, where `rngOf` takes the low ones**, and the difference
is measurable.  A linear congruential generator's low bits cycle with
short periods, which a *spectrum* does not notice — white noise
measured flat either way — and a *threshold test* very much does:
`dust 200.0` fired 115 times in half a second where it should have
fired 100, and every density was high by the same 15%.  Taking bits 15
upward instead costs one division: 98 of 100, 407 of 400, 752 of 800 —
within the Poisson noise of the counts themselves.

**Twenty-four bits, not sixteen, and the sixteen were a bug at every
real sample rate.**  `dust`'s chance per sample is `density /
sampleRate`, which at 44100 Hz and a density of one event a second is
2.3e-5 — smaller than a 16-bit draw's smallest nonzero value of 1.5e-5.
So only the draw *zero* cleared the threshold, and its height is
`0 / p`, which is **zero**: measured, `dust` was silent below 0.673
events a second and quantised to multiples of it above — 0.673, 0.7 and
1.0 all fired 0.67 times a second, and a density of 5.0 fired 1.35.

The tests did not catch it because they run at 6 to 8 kHz, where `p` is
five to seven times larger and the resolution reaches.  A parameter that
works at test rates and not at the rate anybody listens at is the worst
kind, so this reaches to a density of 0.003 events a second at 44100 and
still discards the seven low bits the paragraph above is about.


#### `rngPer`

```
rngPer : Rng -> Float -> Rng
```

The generator, advanced once per instant of *whatever signal it is
given*.  `dust`'s density is a signal, so the fold needs one to run on
and the density is the one it has; the value is ignored here and read
by `dustAt` in the `zip` beside it.


#### `dustAt`

```
dustAt : Rng -> Float -> Float
```

One impulse or none, at this instant's density.  The chance per sample
is `density / sampleRate`; the draw that cleared it is also the
impulse's height, rescaled so the heights are uniform over 0..1 rather
than crowded against a small threshold.


#### `dustOf`

```
dustOf : Float -> Rng -> Float
```

### Filters


#### `OnePoleIn`  <sub>data</sub>

```
OnePoleIn := OnePoleIn Float Float
```

The one-pole coefficient for a cutoff in hertz, clamped to a range where
the feedback cannot diverge.
One sample of the one-pole, with the cutoff arriving per sample so it
may vary — the same `y + k * (x - y)` `audio.ges`'s `lowpass` folds with
a fixed `k`.
**Its own record, not `Both`.**  A constructor's layout is chosen by
*tag*, so one used at two instantiations in a single graph collides in
the code generator — `Both Float Float` here and `Both Gate Key` in a
`voices` bank is one tag with two shapes, and `fmpoly.ges` stopped
building with `insertvalue operand and field disagree in type`.  That is
the same defect `quartet.ges` records about two `Played`s, and it is why
`SvfIn` and `LadderIn` are their own types rather than pairs.


Two integrator states, and the three outputs the last sample produced.

The outputs are *stored* rather than recomputed because the whole point
of this topology is that lowpass, bandpass and highpass fall out of one
pass — recomputing would be running the filter three times to hear it
once.

**`sin w` and not `1 - r`**, and the difference is the whole point of
normalising at all.  The impulse response is `g * r^n * sin((n+1)w) /
sin w`, so its peak is `g / sin w`: with `g = 1 - r` the peak *falls* as
the decay lengthens — measured 0.087 at 0.05 s and 0.0006 at 8 s, a
factor of 140 — and a mode's `level` would have meant nothing.  With
`g = sin w` the peak is within a few percent of 1 whatever the decay,
so `0.7 * resonate …` is a mode at 0.7.

operator.  A record because a `zip`'s step takes one value, and this is
the flat shape the engine lays out — the same reason `SvfIn` is one, and
it lives down here for the same reason too.


#### `Fm`  <sub>data</sub>

```
Fm := Fm Quad Quad
```

An operator bank's state: four phases, and the four outputs of the
previous sample that the wiring reads.

**Every operator reads the previous sample's outputs**, which is what
makes an arbitrary wiring meaningful at all — a cycle in the matrix
would otherwise be a value defined in terms of itself — and it is also
exactly how feedback works on the hardware.  One sample of delay around
every loop, 23 microseconds at 44.1 kHz, inaudible.


#### `fmZero`

```
fmZero : Fm
```


#### `fmNext`

```
fmNext : Patch -> Fm -> Drive -> Fm
```

One sample of the whole bank.  `fm` is what `scan`s this.


#### `fmOut`

```
fmOut : Patch -> Fm -> Float
```

The bank's sample: each operator's output times its share of the mix.
